## 🎯 Learning Objectives

::: {style="font-size: 32px"}
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

- **Derive** the Dickey–Fuller limit of $T(\hat\rho-1)$ from the FCLT, and explain why it is pivotal

- **Carry out** the DF test with the right deterministic terms and the right critical values

- **Correct** for serially correlated errors, nonparametrically (Phillips–Perron) or parametrically (ADF)

- **Interpret** a unit-root verdict as a statement about the persistence of shocks, and its limits
:::

## 🔁 Warm-up from last time {.quiz-question}

Lecture 9: $y_t=y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, $y_0=0$, $\varepsilon_t$ i.i.d.$(0,\sigma^2)$. What is the limit of $\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t$?

- [$\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\{\chi^2(1)-1\}$]{.correct data-explanation="✅ Telescoping gives Σ y_{t−1}ε_t = ½{y_T² − Σε_t²}. Divided by T: y_T²/T → σ²χ²(1) and Σε_t²/T → σ². In Brownian form this is σ²∫B dB = (σ²/2)(B(1)² − 1)."}
- $N(0,\sigma^4)$, as in the stationary case
- $0$, because $E(y_{t-1}\varepsilon_t)=0$
- $\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\chi^2(1)$

---

## 🗺️ Where We Are

::: {style="font-size: 32px"}
Lecture 9 ended on a limit:
$$T(\hat\rho-1)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \frac{\int_0^1 \mathcal B\,d\mathcal B}{\int_0^1 \mathcal B(r)^2dr}.$$
It is non-normal, skewed to the left, and free of $\sigma^2$.

::: {.fragment}
Today that limit becomes a **test**. Three questions decide whether the test is usable in practice: which deterministic terms enter the regression, what to do when the errors are serially correlated, and what a rejection or non-rejection actually tells us.
:::
:::

---

## ❓ The Question

::: {.callout-important}
## Are recessions forgotten?
US real GDP fell about 4% in 2008–09. Does log GDP return to its old trend line, or is the loss carried forward for ever?
:::

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
If log GDP is **trend-stationary**, a shock dies out and the old path returns. If it has a **unit root**, every shock shifts the whole future path, and "returning to trend" has no meaning. The two views give the same short-run forecasts and very different long-run ones.
:::

---

## 📐 Random-Walk Moments (FCLT)

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Let $\varepsilon_t$ be white noise with variance $\sigma^2$ and $x_t=x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$. With $S_T(r)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt T}\,x_{[Tr]}$,
$$S_T(r)\ \Rightarrow\ \mathcal B(r)\quad\text{(standard Brownian motion on }[0,1]),$$
$$\frac1T\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_{t-1}\varepsilon_t\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \sigma^2\!\int_0^1\!\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B,\qquad
\frac1{T^2}\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_{t-1}^2\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \sigma^2\!\int_0^1\!\mathcal B(r)^2dr,$$
jointly.

- **Remark 1.** The same holds for weak white noise that is a martingale difference sequence; the limit still has independent increments.
- **Remark 2.** It holds for $x_0\neq0$, even random, provided $x_0$ is bounded in probability.
:::

---

## 📐 OLS Under a Unit Root

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Model $x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ with $\rho=1$. The OLS estimator is
$$\hat\rho=\frac{\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_tx_{t-1}}{\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_{t-1}^2}=1+\frac{\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_{t-1}\varepsilon_t}{\sum_{t=2}^{T}x_{t-1}^2}.$$

::: {.fragment}
Scale the numerator by $T$ and the denominator by $T^2$:
$$T(\hat\rho-1)=\frac{\frac1T\sum x_{t-1}\varepsilon_t}{\frac1{T^2}\sum x_{t-1}^2}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \underbrace{\frac{\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B}{\int_0^1\mathcal B(r)^2\,dr}}_{DF\ \text{distribution}}.$$
The $\sigma^2$ cancels. The rate is $T$, not $\sqrt T$: $\hat\rho$ is **superconsistent**.
:::
:::

---

## 📐 Pivotal, and Skewed to the Left

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Compare the stationary case, $|\rho|<1$:
$$\sqrt T(\hat\rho-\rho)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,\,1-\rho^2).$$
This limit depends on $\rho$: it is **non-pivotal**, and we must standardise before tabulating.

::: {.fragment}
The DF distribution contains no unknown parameter: it is **pivotal**, and can be tabulated once, by simulation.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Its shape: the numerator is $\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B=\tfrac12\{\mathcal B(1)^2-1\}$, and the denominator is positive, so
$$P\big(T(\hat\rho-1)<0\big)\to P\big(\chi^2(1)<1\big)\approx0.68.$$
Two thirds of the mass lies below zero: $\hat\rho$ is biased downwards.
:::
:::

---

## 📐 The Dickey–Fuller Test

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
$$H_0:\ \rho=1\ \text{(unit root)}\qquad\text{vs}\qquad H_A:\ \rho<1\ \text{(stationarity)}$$

The test is one-sided and **left-tailed**. Two statistics:

- the coefficient statistic: reject $H_0$ if $T(\hat\rho-1)<q_\alpha^{DF}$;
- the $t$-ratio,
$$\tau=\frac{\hat\rho-1}{SE(\hat\rho)}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \frac{\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B}{\big(\int_0^1\mathcal B(r)^2dr\big)^{1/2}}=DF_\tau ,$$
and reject if $\tau<q_\alpha^{DF_\tau}$.

::: {.fragment}
$\tau$ is the ordinary OLS $t$-statistic. Only its reference distribution changes: $DF_\tau$, not $N(0,1)$.
:::
:::

---

## 💻 Simulating the DF Distributions

```{r}
#| label: df-sim
#| code-summary: "📦 10,000 random walks, three DF regressions each"
#| results: hold
df_stats <- function(x, det) {             # returns T(rho_hat - 1) and tau
  y <- x[-1]; xl <- x[-length(x)]; n <- length(y)
  X <- switch(det, none  = cbind(xl), const = cbind(1, xl),
                   trend = cbind(1, seq_len(n), xl))
  fit <- .lm.fit(X, y); k <- ncol(X); b <- fit$coefficients[k]
  se  <- sqrt(sum(fit$residuals^2) / (n - k) * solve(crossprod(X))[k, k])
  c(n * (b - 1), (b - 1) / se)
}
T <- 500; R <- 10000
sims <- t(replicate(R, { x <- cumsum(rnorm(T))
  c(df_stats(x, "none"), df_stats(x, "const"), df_stats(x, "trend")) }))
colnames(sims) <- c("rho_none", "tau_none", "rho_const", "tau_const",
                    "rho_trend", "tau_trend")
round(apply(sims, 2, quantile, c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10)), 2)
mean(sims[, "rho_none"] < 0)               # theory: P(chi2(1) < 1) = 0.683
```

---

## 📊 DF Is Not N(0,1)

```{r}
#| label: df-fig
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.0
dd <- data.frame(tau = c(sims[, "tau_none"], sims[, "tau_const"], sims[, "tau_trend"]),
                 reg = rep(c("no constant", "constant", "constant + trend"), each = R))
dd$reg <- factor(dd$reg, levels = c("no constant", "constant", "constant + trend"))
ggplot(dd, aes(tau, colour = reg)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.2) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, colour = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1.645, colour = "black", linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2f4b7c", "#8b2635", "#d18f2e"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-5.5, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(tau == (hat(rho) - 1) / SE(hat(rho))), y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Dashed: $N(0,1)$; dotted: its 5% point, $-1.645$. Each DF density lies left of the normal, further left with each deterministic term.
:::

---

## 📐 Adding a Constant

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Regress $x_t=\mu+\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ by OLS, obtaining $(\hat\mu,\hat\rho)$. Under $\rho=1$,
$$T(\hat\rho-1)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \frac{\int_0^1\bar{\mathcal B}(r)\,d\bar{\mathcal B}(r)}{\int_0^1\bar{\mathcal B}(r)^2\,dr}=\overline{DF},
\qquad \bar{\mathcal B}(r)=\mathcal B(r)-\int_0^1\mathcal B(s)\,ds .$$

::: {.fragment}
$\bar{\mathcal B}$ is the **demeaned** Brownian motion: estimating $\mu$ is the continuous-time analogue of subtracting the sample mean from $x_{t-1}$.

The limit depends on **which** deterministic terms are in the regression, never on their true values. It is again pivotal.
:::
:::

---

## 📐 Adding a Trend

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Regress $x_t=\mu+\delta t+\rho x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, obtaining $(\hat\mu,\hat\delta,\hat\rho)$. Under $\rho=1$,
$$T(\hat\rho-1)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \frac{\int_0^1\tilde{\mathcal B}(r)\,d\tilde{\mathcal B}(r)}{\int_0^1\tilde{\mathcal B}(r)^2\,dr}=\widetilde{DF},
\qquad \tilde{\mathcal B}(r)=\mathcal B(r)-b_0-b_1r,$$
$$\begin{pmatrix}b_0\\ b_1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\int_0^1(4-6r)\,\mathcal B(r)\,dr\\[2pt] \int_0^1(12r-6)\,\mathcal B(r)\,dr\end{pmatrix}.$$

::: {.fragment}
$b_0+b_1r$ is the least-squares projection of $\mathcal B$ on $\{1,r\}$ in $L^2[0,1]$: $\tilde{\mathcal B}$ is $\mathcal B$ with its own best-fitting line removed.
:::
:::

---

## 📋 Critical Values

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Asymptotic critical values (MacKinnon, 1996), left tail:

| | $T(\hat\rho-1)$, 1% | 5% | 10% | $\tau$, 1% | 5% | 10% |
|:--------------------------|------:|-----:|-----:|------:|-----:|-----:|
| $DF$: no constant | −13.8 | −8.1 | −5.7 | −2.57 | −1.94 | −1.62 |
| $\overline{DF}$: constant | −20.7 | −14.1 | −11.3 | −3.43 | −2.86 | −2.57 |
| $\widetilde{DF}$: + trend | −29.5 | −21.8 | −18.3 | −3.96 | −3.41 | −3.13 |

::: {.fragment}
The simulation two slides back, with $T=500$, reproduces each entry to within about 0.5 for $T(\hat\rho-1)$ and 0.05 for $\tau$. More deterministic terms push the critical values further left.
:::
:::

---

## 🔧 Which Deterministic Terms?

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
- **Always include a constant**, unless the mean has already been removed from the series.
- **A trend depends on the situation**: include it when the series trends, so that the stationary alternative is "stationary around a line".

| Do not include a time trend | Include a time trend |
|---|---|
| inflation, unemployment, interest rates, exchange rates | log GNP, log industrial production, log prices |

::: {.fragment}
Leaving a trend out of a trending series biases the test towards the unit root. Adding one needlessly costs power.
:::
:::

---

## ✍️ Worked Example: A DF Regression

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Quarterly log real GDP, $T=200$. With a constant and a trend, OLS gives $\hat\rho=0.9620$, $SE(\hat\rho)=0.0175$.

::: {.fragment}
**Step 1.** Coefficient statistic: $T(\hat\rho-1)=200\times(-0.0380)=-7.6$.

**Step 2.** $t$-ratio: $\tau=-0.0380/0.0175=-2.17$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Step 3.** Compare with the constant + trend row: $-7.6>-21.8$ and $-2.17>-3.41$. **Do not reject** the unit root at 5%.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The trap.** Against $N(0,1)$, $\tau=-2.17<-1.645$ would "reject". The normal table overstates the evidence against a unit root.
:::
:::

---

## 📐 Serially Correlated Errors

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Return to $x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+u_t$, $\rho=1$. If the true process is not a random walk, $u_t=\Delta x_t$ is **serially correlated**. Write
$$\Gamma_j=E(u_tu_{t-j}),\qquad \omega^2=\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}\Gamma_j,\qquad \lambda=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\Gamma_j=\frac{\omega^2-\Gamma_0}{2}.$$

::: {.fragment}
With $\mathcal B$ now the Brownian motion from the FCLT normalised by $\omega$,
$$T(\hat\rho-1)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \frac{\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B+\lambda/\omega^2}{\int_0^1\mathcal B(r)^2\,dr}.$$
The extra term depends on nuisance parameters, so the DF tables no longer apply.
:::
:::

---

## 📐 Two Remedies

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
**Nonparametric: Phillips–Perron.** Subtract the bias directly:
$$Z=T(\hat\rho-1)-\frac{\hat\lambda}{\frac1{T^2}\sum x_{t-1}^2}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ DF .$$
$\hat\lambda=(\hat\omega^2-\hat\Gamma_0)/2$ uses a Newey–West estimate $\hat\omega^2$. A one-sided sum need not be positive, so no positive-definite estimate of $\lambda$ is required.

::: {.fragment}
**Parametric: augmented Dickey–Fuller.** Add lagged differences:
$$x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\alpha_j\,\underbrace{\Delta x_{t-j}}_{\text{stationary}}+\underbrace{\varepsilon_t}_{\text{pre-whitened}} .$$
Choose $p$ by BIC. Then $ADF=\dfrac{T(\hat\rho-1)}{1-\sum_j\hat\alpha_j}\xrightarrow{d}DF$, and the $t$-ratio on $\rho$ $\xrightarrow{d}DF_\tau$.
:::
:::

---

## 💻 Does the Correction Work?

```{r}
#| label: pp-adf
#| code-summary: "📦 Random walk with MA(1) increments: rejection rates at 5%"
nw_lrv <- function(u, L = floor(4 * (length(u) / 100)^(2 / 9))) {
  n <- length(u); g <- sapply(0:L, function(j) sum(u[(j + 1):n] * u[1:(n - j)]) / n)
  g[1] + 2 * sum((1 - (1:L) / (L + 1)) * g[-1])            # Bartlett kernel
}
stats3 <- function(x, pmax = 8) {          # all with a constant
  y <- x[-1]; xl <- x[-length(x)]; n <- length(y)
  f <- .lm.fit(cbind(1, xl), y); dfz <- n * (f$coefficients[2] - 1)
  lam <- (nw_lrv(f$residuals) - mean(f$residuals^2)) / 2
  pp <- dfz - lam / (sum((xl - mean(xl))^2) / n^2)
  dx <- diff(x); fitp <- function(p, i) { X <- cbind(x[i - 1], 1)
    if (p > 0) for (j in 1:p) X <- cbind(X, dx[i - 1 - j]); .lm.fit(X, x[i]) }
  i0 <- (pmax + 2):length(x)
  bic <- sapply(0:pmax, function(p) length(i0) * log(mean(fitp(p, i0)$residuals^2)) + (p + 2) * log(length(i0)))
  p <- which.min(bic) - 1; i <- (p + 2):length(x); b <- fitp(p, i)$coefficients
  adf <- length(i) * (b[1] - 1) / (1 - if (p > 0) sum(b[3:(p + 2)]) else 0)
  c(DF = dfz, PP = pp, ADF = adf)
}
rate <- function(theta, R = 2000, T = 200) { r <- t(replicate(R, {
  e <- rnorm(T + 1); stats3(cumsum(e[-1] + theta * e[-(T + 1)])) }))
  round(colMeans(r < -14.1), 3) }               # -14.1 = 5% point of DF-bar
rbind(`theta = -0.5` = rate(-0.5), `theta = 0` = rate(0), `theta = +0.5` = rate(0.5))
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Under $H_0$ every entry should be 0.05. Uncorrected DF fails badly; ADF comes closest.
:::

## 🧠 Think–Pair–Share

```{r}
#| label: tps-timer
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(minutes = 3, seconds = 0, top = 0, right = 0,
                     font_size = "2em", warn_when = 30)
```

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
Two processes, driven by the **same** shocks, $T=300$:
$$\text{(A)}\ x_t=x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\qquad \text{(B)}\ x_t=0.999\,x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t .$$

1. After a unit shock, how much remains in (B) after 10 periods? After 700?
2. Would a DF test at 5% tell (A) and (B) apart? Guess the rejection rate under (B).
3. Which of the two do you want for a 4-quarter GDP forecast? For a 50-year pension forecast?
:::

---

## ✅ Think–Pair–Share: Solution

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
1. In (B) the impulse response is $0.999^h$: $0.999^{10}=0.990$, $0.999^{700}=0.496$. The half-life is $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.999\approx693$ periods. In (A) the whole shock remains for ever.

::: {.fragment}
2. No. With $T=300$ the two are practically indistinguishable; the rejection rate under (B) is barely above the 5% size (next slide).
:::

::: {.fragment}
3. For four quarters it does not matter: short-run forecasts coincide. For fifty years it matters entirely: (B) reverts to its mean, (A) never does.
:::
:::

## 📈 The Twins: ρ = 1 and ρ = 0.999

```{r}
#| label: twins
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.9
set.seed(2026)
n <- 300; e <- rnorm(n)
xa <- cumsum(e); xb <- as.numeric(stats::filter(e, 0.999, method = "recursive"))
H <- 3000; h <- 1:H
tw <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = 1:n, x = xa, model = "rho = 1", panel = "sample, t = 1..300"),
  data.frame(t = 1:n, x = xb, model = "rho = 0.999", panel = "sample, t = 1..300"),
  data.frame(t = h, x = rep(xa[n], H), model = "rho = 1", panel = "forecast, h = 1..3000"),
  data.frame(t = h, x = 0.999^h * xb[n], model = "rho = 0.999", panel = "forecast, h = 1..3000"))
tw$panel <- factor(tw$panel, levels = unique(tw$panel))
ggplot(tw, aes(t, x, colour = model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#8b2635", "#2f4b7c"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression(x[t])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Same shocks. In the sample the two paths are one line; only the forecasts part company.
:::

---

## 📊 Can a Test Tell Them Apart?

```{r}
#| label: twins-power
#| code-summary: "📦 DF τ test (constant), 5%: rejection rates, T = 300"
rej <- function(rho, R = 2000) mean(replicate(R, {
  x <- as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(300), rho, method = "recursive"))
  df_stats(x, "const")[2] < -2.86 }))
c(`rho = 1` = rej(1), `rho = 0.999` = rej(0.999), `rho = 0.95` = rej(0.95))
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
At $\rho=0.999$ the test rejects about as often as under the null: its power is essentially its size. Even $\rho=0.95$, a half-life of 14 periods, is missed four times in ten.
:::

## 🎛️ Explore: How Persistent Is ρ?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rho = Inputs.range([0.80, 1.00], {step: 0.005, value: 0.95, label: "ρ"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
shocks = {
  let s = 2026 >>> 0;
  const u = () => { s = (s + 0x6D2B79F5) >>> 0; let t = s;
    t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1); t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61);
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; };
  return Array.from({length: 300}, () => Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(1 - u())) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * u()));
}
pathData = {
  const out = []; let x = 0;
  shocks.forEach((e, i) => { x = rho * x + e; out.push({t: i + 1, x, part: "sample"}); });
  const xT = x;
  for (let h = 1; h <= 300; h++) out.push({t: 300 + h, x: Math.pow(rho, h) * xT, part: "forecast"});
  return out;
}
Plot.plot({
  width: 1100, height: 330, marginLeft: 70, marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "18px"},
  x: {label: "t"}, y: {label: "x_t"},
  color: {domain: ["sample", "forecast"], range: ["#2f4b7c", "#8b2635"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#999"}),
    Plot.ruleX([300], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.line(pathData, {x: "t", y: "x", stroke: "part", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Blue: the sample, same shocks at every $\rho$. Red: the forecast $\rho^h x_T$. As $\rho\to1$ the path stops crossing zero and the forecast stops coming back.
:::

---

## 📐 What a Unit-Root Test Means

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
- The test is about the **persistence** of shocks. Under a unit root, as for log GNP on this view, a shock lasts for ever.
- In a finite sample, $x_t=x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ and $x_t=0.999x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$ cannot be told apart. Their short-run predictions are the same.
- They differ only at long horizons, where the stationary forecast returns to the mean.
- Low power against near-unit-root alternatives is therefore not a defect of a particular test: it is in the problem.
- "Do not reject" means "the data are consistent with very persistent shocks", not "$\rho$ is exactly 1".
:::

---

## 💰 Case Study: Three US Series

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
## 📈 The question

1. Does log real GDP have a unit root around a linear trend?
2. Does the unemployment rate wander, or return to a natural rate?
3. Is the euro–dollar rate a random walk?
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip}
## 📊 The data

**Test**: ADF, lag $p$ by BIC ($p\le12$)

## 💰 Case Study: ADF by Hand

```{r}
#| label: case-adf
#| code-summary: "📦 ADF regression with BIC lag choice, on vendored FRED data"
rd <- function(f) { d <- read.csv(f); d[[2]] <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d[[2]]))
  d <- na.omit(d); d$date <- as.Date(d$observation_date); d }
gdp <- rd("data/GDPC1.csv"); un <- rd("data/UNRATE.csv"); eu <- rd("data/DEXUSEU.csv")
eum <- aggregate(eu$DEXUSEU, list(m = format(eu$date, "%Y-%m")), mean)
adf <- function(x, det, pmax = 12) {
  dx <- diff(x); fitp <- function(p, i) {
    X <- cbind(x[i - 1], 1); if (det == "trend") X <- cbind(X, i)
    if (p > 0) for (j in 1:p) X <- cbind(X, dx[i - 1 - j])
    f <- lm.fit(X, x[i]); s2 <- sum(f$residuals^2) / (length(i) - ncol(X))
    list(f = f, k = ncol(X), se = sqrt(s2 * solve(crossprod(X))[1, 1])) }
  i0 <- (pmax + 2):length(x)
  bic <- sapply(0:pmax, function(p) { r <- fitp(p, i0)
    length(i0) * log(mean(r$f$residuals^2)) + r$k * log(length(i0)) })
  p <- which.min(bic) - 1; r <- fitp(p, (p + 2):length(x)); b <- r$f$coefficients[1]
  c(p = p, T = length(x) - p - 1, rho = round(b, 4), tau = round((b - 1) / r$se, 2),
    crit_5pct = if (det == "trend") -3.41 else -2.86)
}
rbind(log_GDP = adf(log(gdp$GDPC1), "trend"), unemployment = adf(un$UNRATE, "const"),
      log_EURUSD = adf(log(eum$x), "const"))
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
Read the `tau` column against `crit_5pct`: reject the unit root only when `tau` is further left.
:::

## 💰 Case Study: What the Data Say

```{r}
#| label: case-fig
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
lv <- c("log real GDP, OLS trend", "unemployment rate, %", "log USD per EUR")
cs <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = gdp$date, v = log(gdp$GDPC1), s = "log real GDP, OLS trend"),
  data.frame(date = un$date, v = un$UNRATE, s = "unemployment rate, %"),
  data.frame(date = as.Date(paste0(eum$m, "-01")), v = log(eum$x), s = "log USD per EUR"))
tr <- data.frame(date = gdp$date, v = fitted(lm(log(gdp$GDPC1) ~ seq_along(gdp$date))),
                 s = "log real GDP, OLS trend")
cs$s <- factor(cs$s, levels = lv); tr$s <- factor(tr$s, levels = lv)
ggplot(cs, aes(date, v)) + geom_line(colour = "#2f4b7c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = tr, colour = "#8b2635", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ s, scales = "free") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 17))
```

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
**What the data say:** log GDP ($\tau=-1.25$) and the euro ($\tau=-2.08$) do not reject the unit root: GDP stayed below its pre-2008 trend. Unemployment rejects ($\tau=-4.17$): very persistent, yet mean-reverting. A non-rejection is equally consistent with $\rho=0.99$.
:::

## 📝 Quiz #1: Critical Values {.quiz-question}

A DF regression with a constant (no trend) gives $\tau=-2.40$. At the 5% level you should:

- [Not reject the unit root, since $-2.40>-2.86$]{.correct data-explanation="✅ With a constant the reference distribution is DF̄_τ, whose 5% point is −2.86. −2.40 lies to its right, so H0: ρ = 1 is not rejected. The N(0,1) value −1.645 would wrongly reject."}
- Reject the unit root, since $-2.40<-1.645$
- Reject the unit root, since $|-2.40|>1.96$
- Not reject, since $\tau$ must be positive to reject

---

## 📝 Quiz #2: Why ADF Adds Lags {.quiz-question}

In the augmented DF regression $x_t=\rho x_{t-1}+\sum_{j=1}^p\alpha_j\Delta x_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t$, what is the role of the lagged differences?

- [They absorb the serial correlation in $\Delta x_t$, so that $\varepsilon_t$ is serially uncorrelated and the DF tables apply]{.correct data-explanation="✅ Serial correlation adds λ/ω² to the DF limit. The lagged differences pre-whiten the error, and T(ρ̂−1)/(1−Σα̂_j) recovers the DF distribution."}
- They remove the deterministic trend
- They make $x_t$ stationary under the null
- They raise the power against $\rho=0.999$

---

## 📝 Quiz #3: Pivotal {.quiz-question}

Why can the DF distribution be tabulated once and for all, while the stationary limit $N(0,1-\rho^2)$ cannot?

- [The DF limit contains no unknown parameter; the stationary one depends on $\rho$]{.correct data-explanation="✅ In T(ρ̂ − 1) the σ² cancels between numerator and denominator, leaving a functional of standard Brownian motion only. The stationary limit has variance 1 − ρ², which must be estimated and standardised."}
- The DF limit is normal
- The DF limit does not depend on the deterministic terms
- The stationary limit has infinite variance

---

## 📋 Key Formulas

::: {style="font-size: 28px"}
| | |
|---|---|
| DF coefficient | $T(\hat\rho-1)\xrightarrow{d}\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B\big/\int_0^1\mathcal B^2dr$ |
| DF $t$-ratio | $\tau\xrightarrow{d}\int_0^1\mathcal B\,d\mathcal B\big/\big(\int_0^1\mathcal B^2dr\big)^{1/2}$ |
| constant / trend | replace $\mathcal B$ by $\bar{\mathcal B}=\mathcal B-\int\mathcal B$, or $\tilde{\mathcal B}=\mathcal B-b_0-b_1r$ |
| 5% points, $\tau$ | $-1.94$, $-2.86$, $-3.41$ |
| correlated errors | limit gains $+\lambda/\omega^2$ in the numerator, $\lambda=\sum_{j\ge1}\Gamma_j$ |
| Phillips–Perron | $Z=T(\hat\rho-1)-\hat\lambda\big/\big(T^{-2}\sum x_{t-1}^2\big)$ |
| ADF | $T(\hat\rho-1)/(1-\sum_j\hat\alpha_j)$, $p$ by BIC |
:::

---

## 📋 Summary

::: {style="font-size: 30px"}
- Under a unit root $\hat\rho$ converges at rate $T$ to a pivotal, left-skewed DF distribution
- The test is left-tailed; the critical values come from DF tables, never from $N(0,1)$
- Always include a constant; include a trend for trending series
- Serial correlation adds a nuisance term: remove it with Phillips–Perron or with ADF lags
- A unit root and $\rho=0.999$ are indistinguishable in a sample and differ only in the long run
:::
